conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. You're in the ICU because you came in with fever and trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mmm… okay. I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were very sick when you arrived. You’re on a ventilator through your trach to help you breathe. We’re giving you antibiotics for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia again? I just got out of rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we think it’s a new infection. Your sputum culture grew Pseudomonas, a bacteria that can be tough to treat. We started cefepime, which works well against it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful. You’re responding. Your breathing is still labored, but your fever is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth still hurts. The white patches are back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. It’s thrush, a fungal infection. We’re switching from nystatin to fluconazole because it’s stronger and should clear it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my brain? The toxoplasmosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your treatment for toxoplasmosis—pyrimethamine, clindamycin, and leucovorin. You’re on dexamethasone to reduce brain swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need the ventilator long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Right now, you still need support, but we’ll try to wean you as soon as you’re strong enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. We did a bronchoscopy yesterday to get a better sample from your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it helpful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The culture confirmed Pseudomonas. It’s sensitive to cefepime, so we’ll keep that. We also saw a small amount of another bacteria, Stenotrophomonas, but it’s likely not causing infection now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can’t treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d normally use Bactrim, but you’re allergic. So for now, we’ll watch it. Your ID doctor will check at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is better today. We’re starting to reduce ventilator support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any news on my heart? I remember something about an abnormal ECG.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a Brugada pattern on ECG, but cardiology reviewed it. They think it’s due to your illness and fever, not a heart problem. No treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my urine? I had a catheter issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT showed your bladder was very full and inflamed. We think it’s due to obstruction or infection. Your urine culture also grew Pseudomonas, so we’re covering it with cefepime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your stool tests came back negative. No C. diff, parasites, or other infections. Your diarrhea isn’t infectious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely due to your chronic HIV-related gut issues. We’ll keep managing it with your current bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on Truvada and darunavir/ritonavir. We’re also continuing azithromycin and atovaquone for pneumonia prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing even better. You’re now on a trach mask—no ventilator. Big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. When can I go back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aiming for discharge in a couple of days. You’ll go back to extended care, but not yet to full rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the CMV and HSV pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on valganciclovir for that. You’ll continue it until your next follow-up. It’s important to finish the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat MRI of the brain shows your toxoplasmosis lesions are stable. The swelling around them has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the dexamethasone is helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll keep it for now. Your neurologist will decide when to taper it during your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sodium? I remember it was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it dipped into the 130s. We stopped free water flushes. We’ll check your electrolytes weekly and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s a big day. You’ve been off the ventilator for 48 hours. We’re confident you can go to extended care tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue cefepime for 14 days total—so 7 more days. Fluconazole for thrush, then switch back to nystatin. And all your HIV and toxoplasmosis meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dexamethasone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue 2 mg twice daily. Don’t stop it—your neurologist will guide the taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with my trach and feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the facility will manage your trach and PEG tube. They’ll help with mobility and range of motion too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with infectious disease and neurology. They’ll review your MRI results and adjust your treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to discharge. You’ve made excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Keep up with your meds, attend follow-ups, and call if you have fever, trouble breathing, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The rehab team will get you settled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—will I get pneumonia again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your risk is higher due to your weakened immune system, but staying on your preventive meds and attending check-ups will help protect you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to see you improving. The transport team will take you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, ready when they are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep building your strength. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital now because you came in with fever and trouble breathing. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was at the rehab center. Then I fell out of bed. My sister said I wasn’t breathing right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. You were having trouble with secretions and low oxygen. We had to put you on a ventilator to help you breathe. You’ve been sedated, so you might not remember much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ventilator? Like a breathing machine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You have a trach tube, and the machine is helping you. We’re treating you for a lung infection and also found you have a serious intestinal infection called C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: C. diff again? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and this time it’s severe. We’re giving you vancomycin by mouth and metronidazole through your IV to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what about my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating you for pneumonia. Tests from the other hospital showed MRSA and Pseudomonas. So we’re using vancomycin and cefepime—strong antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas… I’ve had that before too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re making sure we cover it well. Your breathing is improving. We’ll keep you on the ventilator for now but hope to wean you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sister mentioned you weren’t moving your right side. We checked your strength, and you’re weaker than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t feel it well. My hip hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to get a CT of your head and an MRI to check your brain. Your EEG didn’t show seizures, but we’re seeing signs of encephalopathy—brain swelling from your HIV and past toxoplasmosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Toxo again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI shows your toxoplasmosis is actually improving. No new lesions. But the brain swelling could explain the weakness. We’re restarting Keppra to prevent seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is getting better. The lung opacities are clearing. That means the pneumonia and fluid in your lungs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But my hip still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered an X-ray. Let me check the results…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist just called. You have a fracture in your right hip—intertrochanteric. That explains the pain. It likely happened when you fell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fracture? I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Orthopedics will do an ORIF—open reduction and internal fixation—with a nail. But we need to wait until you’re more alert and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium was high—hypernatremia. We’ve been giving you free water flushes through your G-tube. It’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was thirsty before I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re monitoring it closely. Also, we placed a PICC line in your arm so we can give antibiotics longer without changing IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is stronger. We’re starting to reduce the ventilator support. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I come off it soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working toward that. First, we’ll try short periods off, then see how you do. Your lungs are healing, but it takes time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We confirmed the hip fracture on X-ray. Ortho wants to operate tomorrow. You’re stable enough now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be able to walk again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. You were starting to walk with a walker before. After surgery and rehab, you should regain strength. But it’ll take weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Surgery went well. They put in an intramedullary nail. You’ll have a dressing and need to keep weight off the leg for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you oxycodone for pain. Let us know if it’s not enough. The incision looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief episode of fast heart rate yesterday—SVT. It resolved with carotid massage. We started metoprolol to prevent it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart raced?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It happened again today, but adenosine fixed it. Echo showed your heart is structurally normal. Metoprolol should help keep it stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing a trial off the ventilator today. If you do well, we can switch to trach mask support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to breathe on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great! You stayed off for four hours. We’ll keep you on the trach mask with 40% oxygen. Much better than the ventilator.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has improved. We’ll keep the vancomycin and metronidazole for another week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows the hip fracture is healing. There’s minimal callus, but no hardware issues. Possible avascular necrosis, but it’s unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the bone might not get enough blood. But it’s not new. We’ll monitor it with your ortho follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making progress. You’re off the ventilator, your infection is clearing, and your hip is healing. We’re planning for discharge in about two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To extended care—similar to your last rehab. You’ll need physical therapy for your hip and to regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HIV labs came back. CD4 is 13, viral load is undetectable. That’s good. We kept you on Truvada and darunavir/ritonavir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been taking them regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But this time, your viral load is low. We need to keep it that way. Please take your meds every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ortho removed your sutures. The wound is healing well. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start PT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll start tomorrow. You’ll work on sitting, standing, and eventually walking with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff treatment is almost done. Finish the full course to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up X-ray shows the hip is stable. Call ortho in six weeks for a check-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re breathing well on the trach mask. We’ll keep it for now, but your lung function is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go to extended care on Thursday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What meds will I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HIV meds, atovaquone and azithromycin for prevention, metoprolol for your heart, Keppra for seizures, and loperamide if you have diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the vancomycin and metronidazole at the facility. After that, no more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert, breathing well, and your infections are treated. Your hip is healing. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. Keep up with PT, take your meds, and follow up with ID and ortho.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You worked hard. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I come back here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if needed. But your team will monitor you. Call if you have fever, trouble breathing, or hip pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your lung scans showed chronic changes. Your PCP might discuss a biopsy later, but not now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll ask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re stopping the fluconazole. Your thrush is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My mouth feels better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re ready to go. The transport team will take you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep getting stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your trach mask is at 40%. Breathe easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feels normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. I know you can’t speak right now because of your trach, but I’m here to help you. You were brought in today because you were having trouble breathing and had a fever. Can you nod if you understand?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve started you on a ventilator to help with your breathing. Your oxygen levels were low, and your chest X-ray showed some new areas of infection in both lungs. Given your history, we’re treating this as a healthcare-associated pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we caught it early. You’re in the ICU for close monitoring. We’ve started IV antibiotics—vancomycin, cefepime, and zosyn—to cover the most likely bacteria. We also gave you Tamiflu just in case there’s a virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on the ventilator long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess daily. Right now, you need it because your breathing is fast and labored. But if your secretions improve and your oxygen gets better, we can try to wean you off soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your HIV medications—darunavir, Truvada, and ritonavir. It’s very important to keep taking them. We also restarted your PCP and MAC prophylaxis with atovaquone and azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Seizure meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Keppra is running on schedule. No signs of seizures. We’ll keep it going since your past seizures were linked to toxoplasmosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a bronchoscopy today to get a better sample from your lungs. It’s called a mini-BAL. It helps us find out exactly what’s causing the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it went well. You tolerated it fine. We’ll get results in a day or two. In the meantime, we’re suctioning your trach regularly to clear thick mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your white blood cell count is still high, which means the infection is active. But your kidney and liver functions are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a low-grade fever overnight, but we gave Tylenol. Your temperature is normal now. The sputum culture from yesterday showed gram-negative rods, but not in large amounts yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it Pseudomonas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for that. The mini-BAL grew two types of gram-negative rods at 10,000–100,000 CFU/mL, which is significant. We’ll keep you on broad coverage for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So still serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you’re responding. Your breathing is a bit easier today. We’re keeping the ventilator settings the same for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line this morning so we can give IV antibiotics for the full course without replacing IVs. It’s in your right arm and should be more comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any news on the tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The viral panel came back negative—no flu, RSV, or other common viruses. CMV and HSV were not found in your BAL. Your C. diff test was negative, so we don’t think it’s colitis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My hip okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hip incision is healing well. No signs of infection. You have a follow-up with ortho next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows some improvement. The edema is mild, and your lung volumes are still low, but not worse. We’re continuing the same treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try off the vent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. But we’re close. Your secretions are still thick, and you desat a bit when we reduce support. We’ll keep suctioning and reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the shadows on my lung?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist noted some focal opacities that could be infection. We’ll repeat the X-ray after a few more days of antibiotics to see if they clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big update: we’re switching your antibiotics. The cultures confirmed gram-negative bacteria, but not Pseudomonas. So we’re changing from vancomycin and cefepime to ceftazidime alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means we can narrow the treatment. You’ll get ceftazidime for 8 days total, unless things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ventilator?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried a trial off the vent today. You did well for 30 minutes. So tomorrow, we’ll try a longer period and see if we can switch you to trach mask support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent news: you’re off the ventilator! You’re now on a trach mask with 50% oxygen. Your breathing is stable, and your oxygen levels are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s amazing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You worked hard. We’ll keep monitoring, but this is a big step. You still need deep suctioning, so we’ll continue that every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still on ceftazidime. You’re on day 5 of 8. We’ll finish the course as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count is coming down. No fever in 48 hours. You’re breathing well on the trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I sit up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll get you out of bed today. Physical therapy will help you sit in a chair. It’s important for your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re off IV antibiotics as of this morning—completed the full 8-day course. We’ll keep your other meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more IVs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just the PICC for now, in case we need it. But no more antibiotics through it. We’ll remove it before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to extended care, not home, because you still need help with suctioning and monitoring. We’re aiming for discharge on Friday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final chest X-ray shows improvement. The opacities are smaller. The mediastinal widening is still there—we recommend a CT later to check your thyroid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thyroid? I didn’t know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we noticed on the X-ray. Could be a goiter. Not urgent, but your primary doctor should follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is tomorrow. You’re stable, off the vent, no fever, and eating through your PEG tube. You’ll continue needing trach care and suctioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds—HIV pills, seizure medicine, stomach protectant, and inhalers as needed. We added ipratropium to help with secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infectious disease, pulmonology, and orthopedics. And your primary doctor for the thyroid check. You’ll also need physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. You’ve done incredibly well. Keep up with your meds and suctioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I know it’s late, but I need to ask you some questions. You were brought in after a fall at your nursing home. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods slowly, points to right leg, then to abdomen*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re having pain in your leg and your belly? Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods vigorously, writes on notepad: 'fell 3 times, pain bad'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any fever, nausea, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *shakes head no, writes: 'no fever, but blood in stool'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We’ll check that. You have a history of HIV and breathing problems, and you’re on a trach. Is that correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, points to trach, writes: 'oxygen ok'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve started you on an antibiotic because your urine test showed an infection. We’ll do some scans to make sure you didn’t hurt yourself when you fell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, looks tired*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scans of your head, neck, chest, and belly are back. No fractures or bleeding. Your old hip surgery looks healed. But your lungs show some chronic changes, nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *points to chest, raises eyebrows*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No pneumonia. Just your usual COPD changes. You’re safe to stay on the trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'good'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We replaced your urinary catheter today. It was due for a change, and since you have a UTI, it’s best to start fresh.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'felt better already'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The antibiotic you got in the ER—ceftriaxone—might not cover the bacteria we’re worried about. So we’re switching you to cefepime, which works better against Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *writes: 'Pseudomonas? bad?'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a tough bacteria, especially with your history. But cefepime should handle it. We’ll give it for 10 days through a new IV line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'ok, thanks'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It’s Pseudomonas, and it’s sensitive to cefepime. That means we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'how long on IV?'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ten days total. You’re on day two. We’ll remove the IV line after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *writes: 'leg pain still there'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but the scans show no new injury. Your leg pain is likely chronic, from your old hip issue. We’ll manage it with pain meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'abdominal pain better'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. The UTI was likely causing that. As the infection clears, the pain should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *smiles slightly*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray today. No signs of pneumonia. Your lungs are clear. You’re doing well on the trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'secretions less'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we lowered the humidity a bit. That helped. Keep using the suction as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *gives thumbs up*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture showed some Staph and Pseudomonas, but only in small amounts. It’s likely just from your usual lung flora, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *writes: 'no new antibiotic?'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not needed. Your current treatment is focused on the UTI. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a midline IV today to make sure you get the full course of cefepime safely. It’ll stay in until your last dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *points to arm, writes: 'ok, not painful'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re responding well. Your sister was updated—she agrees with the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'thank her'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look stable. No signs of sepsis. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *smiles, writes: 'home soon?'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your nursing home. You’ll finish the antibiotics there. A nurse will give the IV doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'ok, good'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’re ready to go. Your UTI is improving, no complications. We’ll send your discharge papers to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, writes: 'thank you'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking the antibiotics as scheduled. Watch for fever or increased pain. And your sister wants urology to check if you still need the catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *writes: 'hope not, uncomfortable'

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll push for that. Take care. If anything changes, call your facility nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, waves goodbye*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I see you came in because your GJ tube was pulled out this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I didn’t mean to. I was moving and it came out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve placed a temporary tube to keep the opening safe. It’s called a Foley catheter, and it’s in your stomach right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get my regular tube back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Interventional Radiology will replace your GJ tube tomorrow. It’s a quick procedure under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just want to get back to my meds and feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you don’t miss anything. For now, you’re getting fluids through an IV, and we gave you a dose of metoprolol because your heart rate was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart? It’s been fast before…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. It’s likely from missing your morning dose and being a bit dehydrated. The IV fluids should help, and we’ll keep you on your usual metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I take a lot of meds… for HIV, seizures, breathing…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed all your medications. You’re on Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir for HIV, Keppra for seizures, and your breathing meds like albuterol. We’ll continue all of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach pain? It’s been off and on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your abdomen. It’s soft, no tenderness. We’ll keep you on hyoscyamine and cholestyramine for your chronic diarrhea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had loose stools again today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We won’t give extra constipation meds unless needed. Your body is adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your lab results. Your white blood cell count was high when you arrived—17,000—but it’s already coming down to 13,000.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but you’re not running a fever or showing other signs. You have a long-term Foley catheter, which often causes bacteria in the urine without being a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. Your urine culture showed mixed bacteria, which means it’s likely contamination. We won’t treat it since you’re not symptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia. It’s likely related to your chronic lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had COPD for years… and the trach helps, but I need suctioning a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re suctioning as needed and giving albuterol if you’re short of breath. Keep using the voice box when you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling? Any pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stomach feels okay. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. You’ll rest tonight, and tomorrow morning the GJ tube will be replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well last night. Your heart rate is down to 69, and your breathing is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Is it time for the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The radiology team replaced your GJ tube this morning under X-ray guidance. It’s in the right place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No incision. They used a wire and a new tube over it. You were given light sedation and tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start my feeds and meds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start slow. The nurse will begin your medications through the tube, then your feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your sister and the nursing home. They said your Foley catheter was kept in place until you finished treatment for a past infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it for over a year…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend removing it soon. It increases infection risk. You could use a condom catheter or urinal instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll talk to the nurse at the home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go back to the extended care facility today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back so soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your tube is fixed, your labs are improving, and you’re stable. Just keep up with your HIV meds, breathing treatments, and follow up with cardiology about your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking it twice a day. But talk to electrophysiology—they can decide if you need it long-term or an ablation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we reviewed your code status with your sister. She said you want full treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I want everything done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. Your care team will respect that. You’ll be discharged in the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is ready. Remember to keep your GJ site clean, take all your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right. Stay well, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Have a safe trip back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—discharge orders are complete. You’re officially discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. See you later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you made it to transport safely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in because you had a fever at the nursing home. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever’s gone down, but I feel weak. They said my heart was racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate was high when you arrived. We gave you fluids, and it’s improved. We’re checking your urine and blood because we think the fever might be from a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a catheter before, but they took it out yesterday. I’ve been peeing on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But sometimes infections can still happen after removal. Your urine test showed signs of infection, so we started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you vancomycin and levofloxacin at first. But we’ll adjust based on the culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Will this affect them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing all your medications. You’re still getting your HIV meds, seizure meds, and breathing treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to miss those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray. It shows some fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia. It might be related to your chronic lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had breathing problems for years. I need suctioning a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping your trach mask on and giving albuterol as needed. We’ll keep an eye on your oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. You have Pseudomonas and Enterococcus. These can be serious, so we’re switching your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those resistant bugs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas can be tough, but your tests show it’s sensitive to cefepime. Enterococcus is being treated with linezolid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cefepime will be IV. We’ll place a PICC line so you can get it at home. Linezolid is oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About two weeks total. You’ll finish the course at the nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still getting Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir daily. Your latest viral load is undetectable, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your citalopram for now. It can interact with linezolid and cause serotonin syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on it for anxiety. Is it safe to restart later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you finish linezolid, you can restart it. We’ll make sure your care team knows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed the PICC line this morning. It went well. You’ll get cefepime through it every 8 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some pressure, but it shouldn’t be painful. We’ll keep it clean and check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the linezolid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a pill you’ll take twice a day. We’ll monitor your blood count in a week to watch for any side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on metoprolol for your fast heart rate. We recommend you follow up with a heart specialist about your SVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. They said it might need ablation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s something to discuss with electrophysiology. We’ll send a note to your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’ve been fever-free, and your white count is coming down. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to the nursing home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’ll continue both antibiotics there. The PICC line will be removed after your last dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your regular medications are listed, including your HIV, seizure, and breathing meds. Restart citalopram after linezolid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your sister and care team get a full update. Call if you develop fever or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , I'll be your doctor during your stay. You're here because you had coffee ground emesis at your nursing home. Can you tell me anything about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes... I saw dark vomit. But I didn’t feel sick. No stomach pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a trach, so you can’t speak easily. We’ll use yes/no head nods. Did you eat anything before the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. NPO. Not supposed to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We checked your PEG tube and the fluid was clear, no blood. Your blood count is stable, so we don’t think you’re bleeding internally. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was high when you arrived—25.5. That’s elevated. But it’s already coming down. We think it might be from your bladder being very full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The CT scan showed your bladder was distended—over a liter of urine. That can trigger a high white count. We drained it with a catheter. You’ll need regular checks to prevent it from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No foley?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. You’ve had many UTIs before, so we avoid long-term catheters. We’ll do intermittent straight catheterizations as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw some inflammation in your bowel on the CT—mild enterocolitis. But no blockage or perforation. Your diarrhea is likely from your chronic C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still on vanco?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Infectious disease recommends continuing oral vancomycin every six hours while on antibiotics, and for two weeks after. This prevents C. diff from flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on IV cefepime and oral linezolid for your recent UTI. The urine culture this time showed no growth, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing them to finish the full course. You’ll complete them at the nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs overnight show your white count normalized. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your hip and knee X-rays. You have avascular necrosis in both hips—bone damage from poor blood flow. The right hip shows early collapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain...

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and there may be some bone changes in your right knee too. Orthopedics reviewed it. They don’t recommend surgery or MRI. You should keep using your walker and do gentle exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. They suggest follow-up in four weeks with repeat X-rays. You’ll work on range of motion with therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Leg pain same. No stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bladder scans are better. You only needed one cath yesterday. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw your hydroureteronephrosis—swelling in the kidneys—has worsened slightly. But it’s likely from the bladder distention, which we’ve addressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Kidneys okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blockage seen. As long as your bladder stays drained, this should improve. No stones were found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today back to the nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue the IV antibiotics for your UTI, and the oral vancomycin for C. diff. We’ll arrange follow-up with orthopedics in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And bladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, regular bladder scans and straight cath if needed. No indwelling catheter due to infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HIV meds are continuing—Darunavir, ritonavir, and Truvada. Your viral load is low, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your citalopram because it can interact with linezolid. Your sister will talk to your psychiatrist about restarting it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert, breathing well on your trach, and no signs of infection. We’re confident you can continue recovering at the nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all instructions to your sister and the facility. She’s listed as your emergency contact and guardian.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any questions before we finalize discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. All clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The transport team will take you back soon. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You were brought in last night because you were having trouble breathing. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Breathing… hard. Chest tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your oxygen levels were low, and you were breathing fast. We’ve got you on extra oxygen through your trach mask, which is helping. We did a chest X-ray, and there’s an infection in the lower part of your right lung—pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia again? Like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but this one is caused by a bacteria called Pseudomonas. It’s common in people with chronic lung issues. We started antibiotics in the ER—vancomycin and cefepime—to cover all possibilities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cefepime… I’ve had that before. For the UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And since it worked before and the bacteria is sensitive to it, we’ll continue it. We’ll give it through an IV every 8 hours for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But my stomach… been loose. Again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a stool test, and yes, you have C. diff again. It’s common after antibiotics. We’re starting oral vancomycin to treat it, just like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take it during the entire cefepime course and for two more weeks after. That helps prevent it from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg pain? It’s worse when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you’ve had chronic right thigh pain. Previous X-rays showed avascular necrosis in your hips. Ortho said surgery isn’t needed now. We’ll keep your regular pain meds—oxycodone and acetaminophen—as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my HIV meds? I missed a few last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your home regimen: Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir daily. Your last viral load was very low, so you’re doing well when you take them. We’ll keep your pneumonia and C. diff treatments separate from these.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll try to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your sputum culture came back. It grew Pseudomonas, but it’s sensitive to cefepime, so we’re on the right track. No changes to antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any resistance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s resistant to ciprofloxacin, but we’re not using that. Cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, and tobramycin all work. We’re sticking with cefepime since it’s already helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the yeast in my sputum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see yeast sometimes in trach patients. It’s not causing infection now, so no treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My breathing feels a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your oxygen is down to 40% now from 50%. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another chest X-ray this morning. The pneumonia looks stable—no worsening. Your blood pressure was a bit low overnight, but it’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt dizzy last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it was from the infection. We’re not changing anything—just keeping an eye on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line in your right arm. It’ll make giving IV antibiotics easier for the full 14 days without changing IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very. We use ultrasound to guide it. After placement, we’ll do a quick X-ray to confirm it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is in and working well. The X-ray shows it ends in the upper part of the big vein near your heart. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hate needle sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing continues to improve. You’re on 35% oxygen now—back to your baseline. We’ll keep the same plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the C. diff? Stools less frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. The vancomycin is working. Remember, keep taking it for two weeks after the cefepime ends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no cholestyramine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. It can bind the vancomycin and make it less effective. You can restart it after finishing the vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs look stable. No fever, white count normal. We’re on track for discharge in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to the facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to extended care. They’ll help with your IV antibiotics through the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back on all your home meds: Keppra for seizures, metoprolol for heart rhythm, citalopram and lorazepam for anxiety, and the rest. We’ve updated the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day in the hospital. You’re breathing well on 35% oxygen, no fever, and your pneumonia is resolving. We’ll discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your facility will coordinate with your doctors—ID for antibiotics, HIV specialist, and ortho for your hip pain. No urgent visits unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’ll stay in until your last dose of cefepime. The nurses at the facility will remove it and care for the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go. You’ve made great progress—back to your baseline. Keep taking all meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. If you develop fever, trouble breathing, or severe diarrhea again, let your team know right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your trach is clear, oxygen at 35%, and you’re alert and moving well. All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you shortly. Keep up the good work with your meds and breathing treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll make sure your records are sent to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. See you later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. You’re doing well. Discharge paperwork is complete.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Feels good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final confirmation: You’re alert, breathing well, and all treatments are set. You’re officially discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate everything. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your doctors here. You were transferred because of increased secretions and trouble breathing. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than this morning. Still coughing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed you’ve had a productive cough and fever. Your blood pressure was low earlier, but fluids helped. We’re concerned about pneumonia again, especially given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia again? Like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, similar. Your chest X-ray shows changes from your chronic lung disease, but it’s hard to tell if there’s new infection. We started antibiotics just in case—Zosyn and vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin? That’s for C. diff too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because you’ve had C. diff before, we’re starting oral vancomycin to prevent it from coming back while you’re on these IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach’s been okay so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep an eye on that. We also saw your urine had a lot of white and red blood cells. We’re checking if that’s a UTI or just colonization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. They said it wasn’t always an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. The culture grew Enterococcus, but it’s likely just colonizing. You’re not having pain or urgency, so we won’t treat it unless it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sputum culture came back. We found Pseudomonas and Klebsiella—both can cause pneumonia in your situation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas again? That’s tough to treat, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but your strain is sensitive to Zosyn, which you're already on. We’re stopping vancomycin since we don’t think you have MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I remember that one had side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on Zosyn for two weeks. Since you’ll need IV antibiotics after discharge, we’re planning to place a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? At the extended care facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The team there can help with the infusions. We want to make sure you finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back. One showed a common skin bacterium, but it’s likely a contaminant. Repeat cultures were negative, so we don’t think you have a bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no endocarditis or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. Your heart exam is clear, and the chest X-ray doesn’t show septic emboli. We’re confident it’s not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your HIV levels. Your viral load is 101 copies/mL, and your CD4 count dropped to 106. It’s higher than your last low, but still shows your immune system is weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I haven’t been great with my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on your current HIV meds—Darunavir, ritonavir, and Truvada. An outpatient ID doctor will help optimize your regimen after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to be more consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did X-rays on your hips today. There’s worsening arthritis in your right hip, which might be contributing to your pain. The avascular necrosis is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been stiff. Hard to move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your right foot is inverted. The X-ray shows no fracture, just bone thinning. Podiatry thinks it’s from being deconditioned. They recommend physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: PT? I haven’t done that in a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it could really help. You’ll have outpatient follow-up with ortho and PT to work on strength and mobility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed this morning. The first X-ray showed it was too far in, so they adjusted it. The new image confirms it’s in the right spot now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pneumothorax or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, everything looks good. No complications. You’ll start IV antibiotics through it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking more stable. Your breathing is easier, and you’re not spiking any fevers. The sputum is still there, but less than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body’s been through a lot. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to the same place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They know your history and can manage your PICC line, antibiotics, and therapy. You’ll continue the oral vancomycin for a week after finishing the IV course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your regular meds—HIV, seizure, stomach, and mental health meds—will continue. We’re switching metoprolol to once daily since your heart rhythm is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the cholestyramine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding that until you finish the oral vancomycin, to avoid interactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s discharge day. You’ve made good progress—stable vitals, improved breathing, and no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the IV Zosyn over the next week, keep taking oral vancomycin for 7 more days after that, and attend your ortho and ID follow-ups. Keep doing your breathing treatments and suctioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And PT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very important. They’ll help with your foot and hip. We’ve included acetaminophen for your joint pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Your sister is listed as your emergency contact and guardian—she’ll be updated. Call us if you develop fever, more secretions, or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital now after coming from your care facility because you had a fever and trouble breathing. I know you can't speak, but I’ll explain what’s going on, and you can nod or point if you need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods slowly, eyes tracking doctor*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your lungs with an X-ray and saw some fluid and congestion. It’s not a new pneumonia like last time. Your trach cuff was also deflated, which might have let secretions build up. We fixed that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *points to neck, then makes a coughing motion*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s why you were breathing fast and had a fever. We gave you antibiotics in the ER and fluids because your blood pressure dropped. You’re stable now. We’re watching your infection closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *gives thumbs up*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine test came back — it showed a lot of Pseudomonas bacteria. That’s likely what caused your fever and low blood pressure, not your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *raises eyebrows, looks concerned*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a urinary tract infection that spread — we call it urosepsis. But you’re already on the right IV antibiotic, Zosyn, which works for this bug. We’ll keep it going for about 8 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods, relaxes shoulders*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started you on oral vancomycin. You’ve had C. diff before, so we’re preventing that while you’re on strong antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *points to stomach, then nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re being careful with your gut. You’ll stay on the vancomycin for a week after the IV antibiotics stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sputum culture also grew Pseudomonas, but only a little. Your lung X-ray shows chronic changes, not a new infection. So we think the main issue is the UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *taps chest, then points to urine bag*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. You’re right — the bacteria were in both places, but the high count in urine and your symptoms point to the bladder as the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *smiles slightly*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is better today. The X-ray from yesterday shows less fluid in your lungs. We’re keeping up with suctioning and your nebulizers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *takes deeper breath, nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your trach tube is a bit off-center — it’s touching the left side of your trachea. ENT will check it soon, but it’s not causing problems now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *touches neck, looks curious*
